report:
Conclusion: The difference (B − A) points toward cooking/culinary language — especially baking/recipes/kitchen/chef/butter/cake — concentrated in middle-to-late layers and in the earliest token positions. This suggests Model B has stronger residual activations for culinary/recipe concepts than Model A (e.g., a domain bias or fine‑tuning on food/recipe text).

Evidence:
- Logit-lens top tokens across many high-norm cells are overwhelmingly culinary: "Cooking", "Cook", "kitchen", "Bake", "Baked", "recipes", "baking", "Chef", "butter", "cake", "vanilla", "Thanksgiving", etc., repeatedly from layers ~17–25 (and many cells in 19–25).
- The L2-norms of the difference are small in early layers and grow large from ~layer 11 onward, peaking strongly in layers 16–25 (especially positions p0 and p1), indicating the signal is represented in mid/late residual stream at early token positions (which is where domain/context bias would influence continuations).
- Some mid‑layers show supporting tokens like "Beyond", "Remember", "Showcase", but the dominant coherent theme in the highest-norm cells is culinary/baking.

Caveats:
- Patchscope continuations are not shown here, so I can’t directly verify behavioural differences (e.g., that B actually generates more recipe text given neutral prompts), only that the residual-stream difference projects toward culinary tokens.
- It could be from fine‑tuning on recipe/food data or a correlated training difference; the evidence supports naming the culinary/recipe domain but not the precise training procedure.
